extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent/trademark/design applicants, and IP practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of substantive requirements, procedural rules and international systems for obtaining and maintaining patents, trademarks, designs, geographical indications and plant variety rights, including deposit and classification rules and international filing routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for patent protection, the invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judged by a person skilled in the art. Prior art (all information disclosed to the public before a given date) assists in determining novelty and inventive step. Patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years) and applicants must disclose their inventions to the public in a manner that enables others skilled in the art to replicate the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing an invention is a generally recognized requirement for receiving a patent; applicants are obliged to disclose inventions so others skilled in the art can replicate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an invention involves a microorganism and cannot be disclosed fully in writing, deposit of a sample (see Budapest Treaty) substitutes for written disclosure. Publication date is the date the application is disclosed to the public and when subject matter becomes prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microorganism deposit (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves a microorganism, national laws in most countries require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA); under the Budapest Treaty the deposit with any IDA is sufficient for patent procedures in all contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDA is a scientific institution (typically a culture collection) capable of storing microorganisms. The Budapest Treaty eliminates need to deposit in every country; deposit suffices for national procedures of contracting states and regional offices recognizing the Treaty. (As of September 2025 there were 52 IDAs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: International Depositary Authority (IDA) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A microorganism deposit must be made with an International Depositary Authority that provides for receipt, acceptance and storage of microorganisms and for furnishing samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDA must have acquired status under the Budapest Treaty. Deposital transmittal and storage are defined functions; applicants should use designated IDAs to meet disclosure obligations for microorganisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT System (international patent filing route)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT facilitates acquisition of patent rights in many jurisdictions by simplifying multiple national filings through an international phase followed by national phase entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International phase includes an international search and possibly a preliminary examination; the national phase consists of entry and processing in individual countries where protection is sought. Decision to grant remains with national/regional patent offices and patent rights remain limited to the jurisdiction of the granting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority (Paris Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Paris Convention establishes the 'right of priority' enabling an IP applicant to claim priority of an earlier application filed up to 12 months previously for patents and utility models, and up to six months previously for trademarks and designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming priority affects filing/priority dates used to assess novelty and prior art; use within time limits is essential to secure priority rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years) and must be maintained to remain in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintenance typically requires payment of renewal/maintenance fees to the relevant IP office; failure to pay may cause lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark substantive function and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another; trademark rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the authority that has registered the trademark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark holders have exclusive right to use the mark for the registered goods/services and can block unauthorized or confusingly similar uses to prevent consumer deception. Trademarks can be registered for goods and services (service marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark maintenance and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided the trademark holder pays required renewal fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark maintenance differs from patents/designs which have limited terms; renewal fees and procedural requirements vary by office and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System (international trademark route)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows trademark applicants to submit a single international application (in English, French or Spanish) indicating the Madrid members where protection is sought, paying one set of fees in Swiss francs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to issue registration remains with each national/regional office; a registration recorded in the International Register has the same effect as a direct registration in each designated Contracting Party unless that authority issues a refusal within a specified time. The System also centralizes management (recording changes, renewals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark class counting and filing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications specify goods/services classes under the Nice Classification; an application can list one or more of 45 classes depending on office procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices may use multi-class or single-class filing systems (some require separate application per class). Comparing class counts helps capture cross-office differences in application/registration numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective versus certification trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective marks distinguish common characteristics of goods/services of different enterprises using the mark and are typically used by members of an association; certification marks are awarded for compliance with defined standards and may be used by anyone who complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main difference in many jurisdictions is use restrictions: collective marks limited to group members, certification marks open to any user meeting the owner's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design protection: novelty/originality and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs (ornamental/aesthetic aspects of articles) can be protected if they are new or original; the holder of a registered design has exclusive rights and can prevent unauthorized copying or imitation. Design registrations are valid for a limited period (usually 15 years, with variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical term: five-year periods renewable up to a total of 15 years in most jurisdictions; some jurisdictions differ (e.g., China provides 10 years from application date). Some countries protect designs via design patents rather than design registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System (international design route)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System enables applicants to register designs in multiple territories by filing a single application with the WIPO International Bureau and allows filing of up to 100 different designs per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System simplifies multinational registration and subsequent management (recording changes, renewals) through a single procedural step for all designated members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design count rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The design count is the number of designs contained in a design application or registration; under the Hague System up to 100 designs per application may be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National/regional offices differ in allowing multiple designs in one application; some allow more than one design for same product or class, others allow only one design per application. Design counts are useful for comparing application/registration numbers across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety protection substantive criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder's right (plant variety protection) is granted only when a variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection, a plant breeder must file an individual application with each authority. Under UPOV standards these are the core criteria for granting breeder's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: US Plant protection regimes (PPA vs PVPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the US, the Plant Patent Act (PPA) covers distinct and new asexually reproduced plant varieties (with certain exclusions like tuber-propagated plants), while the Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) protects sexually reproduced and tuber-propagated plant varieties (excluding fungi and bacteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must select the appropriate legal route depending on reproduction type; the PPA may grant patents for asexually reproduced varieties, PVPA grants breeder's rights for eligible sexually reproduced/tuber-propagated varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) core function and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A GI is a sign identifying a good as originating in a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs mainly apply to agricultural and food products but also to handicrafts and manufactured goods whose qualities stem from local know-how or natural resources. GIs may be place names or traditional non-geographical terms with geographical connotation (e.g., 'ARGANE').

rubrics_metrics.name: GI use conditions and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications can only be used on goods that meet specific predefined requirements concerning geographical origin, production methods, quality and typicity; goods produced elsewhere or not complying with these requirements cannot use the protected indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI protection is territorial; securing protection abroad requires applying under the foreign law or via international agreements/systems (e.g., Lisbon System).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellation of origin (AO) higher linkage requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellation of origin is a specific kind of GI that usually consists of a geographical name where the quality or characteristics of the product are due exclusively or essentially to that origin, including natural and human factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared to other GIs, appellations of origin require a stronger link to place of origin and are a more restrictive sub-category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection tools for GIs (sui generis, trademarks, unfair competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of GIs relies on different tools: many jurisdictions use sui generis systems (specific GI laws often based on registration), others rely on trademark law (collective/certification marks), and GIs may also be protected through unfair competition and consumer protection laws, judicial/administrative decisions, or decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI protection methods are not mutually exclusive and may coexist. Protection is territorial; international agreements and WIPO-administered systems (Lisbon, Madrid) can facilitate protection abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System (international AO/GI registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lisbon System provides for international protection of appellations of origin and, since 2015, also geographical indications through a single registration administered by WIPO; registration ensures protection in all contracting parties for so long as the AO/GI remains protected in its contracting party of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Lisbon member retains the right to refuse protection to a new international registration on any national/regional ground within one year following WIPO notification. The Geneva Act (2015) expanded scope and membership flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: International registration/route limitation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: International systems (Madrid, Hague, Lisbon, PCT, Budapest Treaty) simplify filing and central management but do not replace national/regional substantive examination: the decision to grant protection remains the prerogative of the national or regional IP office, and rights remain territorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An international registration can facilitate filings and management, but applicants must monitor refusals, national time limits, and national procedural requirements (e.g., refusals within specified periods, entry to national phase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification systems (IPC, Locarno, Nice)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPC (patents), Locarno (designs) and Nice (trademarks) are international classification systems used to categorize technical features, designs and goods/services; multiple symbols/classes can be assigned depending on features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC has hierarchical language-independent symbols. Locarno consists of 32 classes and subclasses for designs; Nice has 45 classes (34 goods, 11 services). Classification affects filing, statistics, and comparison across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application/grant concept for regional offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications/grants at regional offices are treated as equivalent to multiple applications/grants, one in each member state of those offices; WIPO multiplies each regional application/grant by the number of member states to calculate equivalent applications/grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different rules apply for different regional offices (examples provided for BOIP, EAPO, OAPI, GCC, EUIPO, EPO, ARIPO) and for counting resident vs non-resident filings. This concept is used for reporting data by origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and renewal (general IP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance (renewal) is the act by the applicant to keep an IP grant/registration valid (in force), primarily by paying required fees to the IP office; failure to pay can cause lapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: maintenance fee, renewal; trademarks can be maintained indefinitely with renewals, while patents, utility models and designs have limited maintenance periods and may require periodic fees until expiry.
